links.label: grew out of blues
links.reason: New Orleans jazz mixed brass-band marches, ragtime and blues with group improvisation, and blues forms and blue notes stayed at its heart.

links.label: grew out of blues
links.reason: Rhythm and blues was shaped by blending blues and jazz with a city sound.

links.label: grew out of blues
links.reason: Chicago electric blues supplied many of rock and roll's elements, and its 12-bar form runs through early hits.

links.label: grew out of blues
links.reason: Rock borrowed the verse-refrain shape of blues, and British bands like the Rolling Stones drew directly on American blues.

links.label: grew out of jazz
links.reason: Rhythm and blues was shaped by blending jazz and blues with a city sound.

links.label: grew out of jazz
links.reason: Funk can be placed in a line running from rhythm and blues, jazz and soul.

links.label: drew on jazz
links.reason: Reggae's precursors drew on American jazz and rhythm and blues alongside Jamaican music.

links.label: jazz met samba
links.reason: Bossa nova took some harmony and instrumentation from jazz, though its rich chords also grew out of samba guitar on a parallel path.

links.label: jazz met salsa
links.reason: Salsa folds in jazz alongside mambo, rumba, bolero and R&B.

links.label: jazz met afrobeat
links.reason: Afrobeat carries American funk, jazz and soul influences.

links.label: grew out of gospel
links.reason: Rhythm and blues mixed gospel with jump blues, swing, boogie and blues, and its stronger gospel influence is what sets it apart from jump blues.

links.label: grew out of gospel
links.reason: Rock and roll's roots include rhythm and blues combined with shouting gospel.

links.label: grew out of gospel
links.reason: Soul music has its roots in African-American gospel music and rhythm and blues.

links.label: grew out of country
links.reason: Rock and roll mixed rhythm and blues with country music; rockabilly drew mainly on those country roots.

links.label: grew out of country
links.reason: Country is listed among rock's roots, alongside folk and rhythm and blues.

links.label: folk met rock
links.reason: Folk rock is usually thought to have taken off when the Byrds, from LA's folk café scene, recorded Dylan's 'Mr. Tambourine Man' with electric guitars and drums in 1965; Dylan went electric later that year.

links.label: grew out of R&B
links.reason: The immediate roots of rock and roll lay in rhythm and blues, then marketed as 'race music'.

links.label: grew out of rock and roll
links.reason: Rock music's foundations are in rock and roll, which by the mid-1960s had grown into a wider international style.

links.label: grew out of rock and roll
links.reason: Punk rock is rooted in 1950s rock and roll and 1960s garage rock.

links.label: grew out of rock
links.reason: Heavy metal is a genre of rock that grew from blues rock and psychedelic rock in the late 1960s.

sources.section: Soft rock, hard rock, and early heavy metal

links.label: pushed back against rock
links.reason: Punk bands rejected the overproduction and corporate feel of mainstream arena rock.

links.label: metal met alternative
links.reason: In the 1990s some bands were credited with making a place for heavy metal inside alternative rock.

links.label: alt-rock grew from punk
links.reason: Alternative rock describes the underground music that emerged in the wake of punk rock.

links.label: synth-pop arose from punk
links.reason: Synth-pop is said to have arisen partly from punk rock.

links.label: soul grew from R&B
links.reason: Soul is rooted in gospel and rhythm and blues, described by AllMusic as R&B made more urban and commercial.

links.label: funk grew from R&B
links.reason: Funk is placed in the lineage of rhythm and blues, jazz and soul, with its rhythmic template in New Orleans R&B.

links.label: reggae drew on R&B
links.reason: Jamaican music developed out of a mix of American R&B and the local mento style on the way to reggae.

links.label: salsa took in R&B
links.reason: Salsa is described as mixing Cuban styles with elements of jazz and R&B.

links.label: modern R&B grew from R&B
links.reason: Contemporary R&B, which developed in the late 1980s, combines rhythm and blues with pop, soul, funk, disco and electronic elements.

links.label: funk emerged from soul
links.reason: James Brown and Sly and the Family Stone moved from soul into funk, and funk vocals keep soul's approach.

links.label: disco grew from soul
links.reason: Philadelphia soul and psychedelic soul are named among disco's roots, and some early-1970s soul records are called a link to disco.

links.label: hip-hop draws on soul
links.reason: Soul is one of the styles hip-hop grew out of.

links.label: Afrobeat took in soul
links.reason: Afrobeat mixes West African music with American funk, jazz and soul influences.

links.label: soul became modern R&B
links.reason: After the early 1980s soul grew slicker under electro's influence, becoming the style known as contemporary R&B.

links.label: disco drew on funk
links.reason: Disco owed a great deal to funk, which is one of its roots.

links.label: hip-hop sampled funk
links.reason: Hip-hop's earliest DJs drew mainly on disco and funk records, and funk breakbeats have been sampled widely ever since.

links.label: funk met African rhythm
links.reason: Exported to Africa, funk melded with African singing and rhythms, and Fela Kuti, heavily influenced by James Brown, is credited with creating Afrobeat.

links.label: electro grew from funk
links.reason: Electro emerged as a fusion of several styles, funk among them.

links.label: R&B folded in funk
links.reason: Contemporary R&B is described as rhythm and blues combined with elements of pop, disco, funk and soul.

links.label: house picked up disco
links.reason: House is described as picking up where disco left off at the end of the 1970s, with disco one of its main influences.

links.label: hip-hop sprang from disco
links.reason: Early Bronx DJs built hip-hop mainly from disco and funk records, and Chic's 'Good Times' became the basis of 'Rapper's Delight'. Much of young hip-hop's early spirit was a rebellion against disco, the music it came from.

links.label: synth-pop borrowed disco
links.reason: Synth-pop is described as drawing on disco and glam rock, forms critics looked down on.

links.label: techno built on disco
links.reason: Techno used the basic disco drum pattern as a foundation, and Italo and Euro disco were party staples in the Detroit scene it came from.

links.label: R&B folded in disco
links.reason: Contemporary R&B is described as rhythm and blues combined with elements of pop, disco, funk and soul.

links.label: garage borrowed R&B vocals
links.reason: UK garage's 2-step style added contemporary R&B-style vocals among its funkier elements.

links.label: R&B met hip-hop
links.reason: Teddy Riley's blend of R&B singing and hip-hop rhythms was named new jack swing, and the two genres have blended ever since.

links.label: remixed into dub
links.reason: Dub grew out of reggae as engineers stripped reggae tracks back to drums and bass and added echo and reverb.

links.label: via Spanish reggae
links.reason: Reggaeton evolved from dancehall and reggae, starting with the Spanish-language reggae of Panama in the late 1980s.

links.label: a digitised offshoot
links.reason: Jungle, the forerunner of drum and bass, has been called a raved-up, digitised offshoot of Jamaican reggae, and Britain's reggae culture helped form it.

links.label: toasting over versions
links.reason: Dub, with its vocal-free 'versions' of records, is called the strongest artistic precedent for hip-hop.

links.label: dub presaged ambient
links.reason: Jamaican dub was one of the styles that came before ambient and pointed the way; ambient is among the genres dub influenced.

links.label: a basis for jungle
links.reason: Dub was a basis for jungle and drum and bass.

links.label: bass and effects
links.reason: Dub was a major influence on dubstep, which shares its focus on bass and audio effects.

links.label: hip-hop meets dancehall
links.reason: Early producers DJ Playero and DJ Nelson were inspired by hip-hop and dancehall, and reggaeton songs follow hip-hop's verse-chorus-bridge structure.

links.label: trap grew out of hip-hop
links.reason: Trap is a subgenre of hip-hop that began in the Southern United States.

links.label: electro met rap
links.reason: Early electro was mostly instrumental but used rap, and electro in turn shaped hip-hop's new school.

links.label: drum and bass borrowed hip-hop
links.reason: Drum and bass drew on elements of reggae, dub and hip-hop.

links.label: trap drums in EDM
links.reason: From 2013 producers such as DJ Snake brought trap-influenced EDM into the mainstream, a fusion known as EDM trap.

links.label: techno-pop into electro
links.reason: Electro grew from funk and boogie mixed with German and Japanese techno-pop, with synth-pop among its roots.

links.label: fed Detroit techno
links.reason: Juan Atkins and others developed Detroit techno from a style influenced by synth-pop and funk.

links.label: an influence on house
links.reason: Synth-pop was a major influence on house music, which grew out of early-1980s post-disco club culture.

links.label: Detroit electro roots
links.reason: Juan Atkins made electro as Cybotron before techno had its name, and many early British techno producers came to it through electro and hip hop.

links.label: electro in the mix
links.reason: Electro is one of house's roots: early Chicago DJs played electro funk by Afrika Bambaataa and Arthur Baker.

sources.section: 1980s: Chicago house, acid house and deep house

links.label: ambient breakdowns
links.reason: Trance incorporates influences from ambient, chill-out and film scores, and its breakdowns drop the beats to leave melody or atmosphere standing alone.

links.label: ambient techno
links.reason: Ambient techno, from the 1990s, set ambient atmospheres over the rhythms and melodies of techno.

links.label: ambient house chill-out
links.reason: Ambient house, from the late 1980s, added ambient atmospheres to acid house, as on chill-out albums like The KLF's Chill Out.

links.label: Chicago–Detroit kinship
links.reason: Detroit's techno producers were closely tied to the Chicago house scene, and German techno was described as a style built on Chicago house.

links.label: house and acid in trance
links.reason: Trance draws on house and acid house as well as techno.

links.label: New York garage, sped up
links.reason: UK garage grew in London from New York garage house, played faster in the second rooms of jungle nights.

links.label: house goes stadium
links.reason: The 2010s US 'EDM' sound was described as somewhere between electro and progressive house, and the Swedish house trio Swedish House Mafia is credited with setting the tone for the early-2010s EDM boom.

links.label: Frankfurt techno turns trance
links.reason: Trance emerged from the techno and EBM scene in Frankfurt in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

links.label: techno in the breakbeats
links.reason: Drum and bass drew on techno among many sources, and Kevin Saunderson's 'Reese' bassline became hugely influential in it.

links.label: jungle's second room
links.reason: UK garage grew partly out of jungle: the garage played in jungle nights' second rooms offered a slower, more soulful alternative.

links.label: drum and bass weight
links.reason: Early dubstep producers set out to bring drum and bass elements, like the bass drop, into the 2-step garage sound.

links.label: dark garage becomes dubstep
links.reason: Dubstep's roots are in the darker, more experimental B-sides of UK garage producers.

links.label: brostep crosses to America
links.reason: In 2011 dubstep took off in the US through Skrillex's harsher brostep, one of the sounds of the EDM boom.

links.label: a parent of pop
links.reason: Early pop music drew on traditional pop, and rock and roll pushed the older style aside in the 1950s.

links.label: swing-era singers
links.reason: After the swing era, singers from the big bands, such as Frank Sinatra and Peggy Lee, went on to be marketed as solo pop singers.

sources.section: Mid-1940s to mid-1950s: height of popularity

links.label: Tin Pan Alley blues
links.reason: In the 1910s and 1920s Tin Pan Alley published pop songs and dance numbers in the newly popular blues and jazz styles.

links.label: Tin Pan Alley's songcraft
links.reason: Rock lyrics took some of their themes from the Tin Pan Alley pop tradition, even as rock and roll pushed traditional pop aside in the 1950s.

links.label: Nashville's pop polish
links.reason: In the late 1950s Nashville country borrowed heavily from traditional pop sounds to hold back rock and roll.

links.label: pop's rock and roll roots
links.reason: In the 1950s and 1960s 'pop' meant rock and roll and the youth styles it influenced, before the two words split.

links.label: pop meets R&B
links.reason: Contemporary R&B blends rhythm and blues with pop, soul, funk and disco.

links.label: pop on synthesizers
links.reason: Synth-pop took pop songs and built them on synthesizers, part of pop's 1980s turn to electronic sounds.

links.label: Korea's take on pop
links.reason: K-pop grew in South Korea under heavy influence from American pop music.

links.label: rap dance roots
links.reason: Seo Taiji and Boys brought rap into Korean pop, and later groups such as BTS kept hip-hop as their musical base.

links.label: techno in the mix
links.reason: K-pop's 'rap dance' beginnings fused hip-hop with techno and rock.

links.label: rock in the mix
links.reason: Rock was one of the Western styles, along with hip-hop and techno, that early K-pop fused together.

links.label: R&B-shaped pop
links.reason: K-pop mixes R&B and other African American influences with Western dance music and hip-hop.

links.label: synthesizer-led idol pop
links.reason: In synth-pop's 21st-century revival, much Korean pop, especially girl groups such as Girls' Generation and Wonder Girls, came to be dominated by synth-pop.

links.label: indie's roots in rock
links.reason: Indie rock is a subgenre of rock, first named for rock bands on independent labels.

links.label: punk's do-it-yourself idea
links.reason: Punk's do-it-yourself ethic, which said anyone could form a band and put out a record, gave indie rock its start.

links.label: post-punk's indie labels
links.reason: Post-punk bands on independent labels such as Rough Trade and Factory were a foundational influence on indie rock.

links.label: began as alternative rock
links.reason: Indie rock first described a style of alternative rock tied to small, low-budget independent labels. Indie rock took shape as a rejection of alternative rock's move into the mainstream in the 1990s.

links.label: grindie crossover
links.reason: Grindie was a fusion of grime with indie rock.

links.label: grew from punk
links.reason: Post-punk came straight out of punk in the late 1970s, and many of its musicians were inspired by punk shows such as the Sex Pistols' 1976 Manchester gigs. Post-punk rejected punk's raw, simple conventions once punk became a commercial formula.

links.label: krautrock's open forms
links.reason: Many post-punk bands named krautrock groups such as Can, Neu! and Faust as key inspirations, and Kraftwerk shaped post-punk production.

links.label: dub's echo and bass
links.reason: Post-punk bands such as PiL and the Slits took up dub's production techniques and heavy bass.

links.label: reggae's rhythms
links.reason: Reggae was one of the non-rock styles post-punk embraced; PiL's Jah Wobble called it a natural influence.

links.label: funk-driven punk
links.reason: Post-punk bands such as Gang of Four mixed funk rhythms into punk, and Talking Heads added funk and Afrobeat.

links.label: open to disco
links.reason: Post-punk was open to disco's beats, and PiL's first album drew on disco as well as dub and noise.

links.label: free jazz edges
links.reason: Avant-garde and free jazz stood out among post-punk's influences, and the Pop Group mixed free jazz with dub reggae.

links.label: darkness from early metal
links.reason: Post-punk absorbed darker, heavier elements from early heavy metal, especially Black Sabbath.

links.label: seeds of alternative rock
links.reason: Post-punk acts that were fixtures on US college radio, such as R.E.M., became early examples of alternative rock, and Siouxsie and the Banshees were among the first alternative bands.

links.label: post-punk goes electronic
links.reason: In the post-punk era, acts such as Gary Numan, the Human League and Depeche Mode pioneered synth-pop as part of the new wave.

links.label: rock, made experimental
links.reason: Krautrock is a branch of experimental rock that drew on British and American acts like the Velvet Underground and Pink Floyd while moving away from rock's blues roots.

links.label: funk rhythm in the mix
links.reason: Krautrock bands folded funk rhythms into their sound, and James Brown was a noted influence; Can's sound has been described as psychedelic funk.

links.label: jazz improvisation absorbed
links.reason: Krautrock borrowed jazz improvisation, from free jazz to Miles Davis's late-1960s fusion records.

links.label: Kraftwerk's road to synth-pop
links.reason: Synth-pop drew on krautrock, especially Kraftwerk's electronic pop.

links.label: kosmische roots of ambient
links.reason: Krautrock's spacey, drone-based side helped lay the ground for ambient music.

links.label: German machines, Detroit techno
links.reason: Krautrock helped shape techno, and Detroit's first techno producers fused Kraftwerk's repetitive melodies with funk.

links.label: krautrock behind industrial
links.reason: Germany's krautrock scene, Kraftwerk included, is counted among the forerunners of industrial music and EBM.

links.label: reggae, stripped back
links.reason: Dancehall began as a sparer version of reggae, with deejays toasting over rhythm tracks taken from 1960s and 1970s reggae songs.

links.label: dub's riddims underneath
links.reason: Dub is one of dancehall's roots: early deejays toasted over bass-and-drum 'dub' rhythm tracks taken from 1960s and 1970s reggae songs.

links.label: dancehall becomes reggaeton
links.reason: Reggaeton evolved from dancehall, and the faster, simpler digital beat of late-1980s dancehall shaped Reggae en Español.

links.label: dancehall feeds jungle
links.reason: Dancehall was a key influence on drum and bass, and jungle tracks sampled its vocals.

sources.section: Genres influenced by drum and bass

links.label: dancehall rhythms in grime
links.reason: Grime draws on dancehall alongside jungle and hip-hop, reworking some of its rhythms.

links.label: dancehall in afrobeats
links.reason: Afrobeats mixes in dancehall along with hip-hop, house and soca.

links.label: son, the base of salsa
links.reason: Most salsa is built mainly on son montuno and son cubano. Its origins are disputed (the first self-named salsa band formed in Cuba in 1955), and it took off in New York in the 1960s and 1970s, played largely by Puerto Rican, Cuban and Dominican musicians.

links.label: son's singing bass lines
links.reason: Arsenio Rodríguez's son conjunto gave the bass its own melodic riff (tumbao), an idea later called critical to Motown, rock and funk.

links.label: samba, made cool
links.reason: Bossa nova began in the late 1950s as a relaxed, non-dancing style of samba, at first called 'modern samba'.

sources.section: Bossa nova, the new revolution in samba

links.label: jazz tones in samba
links.reason: Post-war samba-canção sometimes took on cool-jazz tones, and jazz-samba adapted street samba into jazz.

sources.section: Samba-canção hegemony and influences of foreign music

links.label: samba rhythms on the disco floor
links.reason: Disco borrowed Latin rhythms, samba among them.

links.label: jazz melodies, African metres
links.reason: Highlife lays Western jazz melodies and horns over several local African rhythms.

links.label: highlife into Afrobeat
links.reason: Afrobeat grew from a mix of genres, highlife among them.

links.label: highlife under afrobeats
links.reason: Modern afrobeats grew from West African genres including highlife.

links.label: afrobeat laid the groundwork
links.reason: Fela Kuti and Tony Allen's afrobeat is credited with laying the groundwork, though afrobeats is a looser, less political pop blend.

links.label: hip-hop gets West African
links.reason: Early groups such as Trybesmen and Plantashun Boiz fused American hip-hop and R&B with local melodies, and hip-hop is one of the styles afrobeats blends.

links.label: house tempo, clave beat
links.reason: Afrobeats shares house music's momentum and tempo, and some 2020s songs fuse the two as 'afro-house'.

links.label: trap-tinged 2020s afrobeats
links.reason: Some early-2020s afrobeats carries trap influence in its beats.

links.label: R&B-infused afrobeats
links.reason: R&B runs through afrobeats from its start, and the early-2020s sound of Tems and Rema is defined by it.

links.label: afrobeats meets amapiano
links.reason: Afropiano blends Nigerian afrobeats with South Africa's amapiano and became one of afrobeats' most popular forms in the early 2020s.

links.label: South Africa's house offshoot
links.reason: Amapiano is one of South Africa's offshoots of house, built on deep house and kwaito, itself a slowed-down township house.

links.label: jazz mixed in
links.reason: Amapiano blends in jazz, and kwaito already had a jazz strand, kwai-jazz, developed by Don Laka.

links.label: soulful piano house
links.reason: Soul is one of the styles amapiano is a hybrid of, and its 'private school' strand uses live guitar, sax and violin.

links.label: kwaito meets rap
links.reason: Kwaito drew on hip-hop, and TKZee's 'guz' sound and later skhanda rap put rap-style vocals over kwaito beats.

links.label: disco samples in kwaito
links.reason: Kwaito producers often sampled disco, alongside South African music and hip-hop.

links.label: disco sped up
links.reason: Hi-NRG is uptempo disco, and the name came from Donna Summer describing the 'high energy' of 'I Feel Love'.

links.label: synth-pop meets disco
links.reason: Italo disco grew out of post-disco dance music and synth-pop, and hi-NRG's octave basslines may be traced back to synth-pop.

links.label: high energy into house
links.reason: The hi-NRG sound influenced house, and one strand already drew on early Chicago house.

links.label: hi-NRG feeds techno
links.reason: The hi-NRG sound influenced techno, and Italo disco and Euro disco were popular at the Detroit high-school parties techno came from.

links.label: hi-NRG into nu-NRG trance
links.reason: In the 1990s a form of trance, nu-NRG, grew out of hi-NRG.

links.label: synth-pop into EBM
links.reason: The synth-pop of The Human League and Fad Gadget is among the influences on EBM.

links.label: punk gets electronic
links.reason: EBM grew out of both punk and industrial cultures, as an electronic kind of punk mixed with industrial sounds.

links.label: rock, avant-garde, electronics
links.reason: Industrial's roots include rock alongside the avant-garde and early electronic music, though it rejected rock's conventions.

links.label: disco beats in EBM
links.reason: EBM sets its sequenced basslines over programmed disco rhythms, often the steady 4/4 disco beat.

links.label: EBM meets thrash metal
links.reason: North American bands combined EBM bass sequences with the roughness of hardcore punk and thrash metal, a mix close to industrial metal.

links.label: EBM feeds techno
links.reason: Techno draws on electronic body music and Belgian new beat, and later European techno producers took up EBM again.

links.label: EBM to Frankfurt trance
links.reason: Trance emerged from the techno and EBM scene in Frankfurt, Germany.

links.label: industrial roots of hardcore
links.reason: Hardcore techno is rooted in 1970s and early-1980s industrial music, and EBM is among its origins.

links.label: techno, harder and faster
links.reason: Hardcore is a form of techno; around 1993 it left its Detroit techno influences behind and was simply called hardcore.

links.label: acid house hardens it
links.reason: Under the influence of acid house and Belgian new beat, EBM grew harder, setting the stage for hardcore.

links.label: hardcore into trance
links.reason: Trance drew on hardcore techno among its sources, alongside house, techno and acid house.

links.label: darker garage becomes grime
links.reason: Grime developed out of UK garage, as its darker, instrumental strand left space for MCs and garage moved away from house.

links.label: jungle drums, garage MCs
links.reason: Grime took the thumping drums of drum and bass and jungle, and Dizzee Rascal started out as a drum and bass DJ.

links.label: cousin of hip hop
links.reason: Grime draws on hip-hop and is often compared with it, though it is usually held to be distinct because its roots are in garage and jungle.

links.label: shared London roots
links.reason: Dubstep incorporates elements of grime, and dubstep's rise in the late 2000s made it harder for grime to get noticed.
